body_markdown:
Pontiac and its dealers were basically printing money selling Trans Ams in the mid- and late-1970s. The flashy Firebirds seemed to be *everywhere* . Black ones became especially hot after Burt Reynolds hooned a Trans Am Special Edition to taunt and evade a bumbling, vengeful sheriff in[Smokey and the Bandit ,](https://www.hagerty.com/media/archived/smokey-and-the-bandit-movie-review/) 1977’s second-highest-grossing movie behind “Star Wars.”


Inexplicably, one Starlight Black ’78 Trans Am—not a Special Edition, which had more ornate gold exterior decal trim—languished for months at Suburban Pontiac in Glen Head, New York, on Long Island’s North Shore. Eddie Bloom had his eye on this black ’Bird, and he wanted it badly.


The 24-year-old drag racer had an insider’s advantage. He was working for his father Eli’s dealership, Myrtle Motors in Maspeth, about 20 miles west of Suburban, which was his uncle’s franchise. Part of his job was arranging car swaps between the two dealerships. When Suburban’s sales manager called about a Grand Prix Myrtle had, Eddie seized the opportunity to trade for the Trans Am. Suburban was thrilled to unload it. The car’s order had been screwed up, and the buyer walked when it arrived lacking some of the options he’d requested. While it was a disappointment for the would-be buyer, it had the two things Eddie wanted most: a four-speed stick and a solid roof.


The four-speed only came with the W72 motor in 1977-1979 Trans Ams.


Courtesy Eddie Bloom


“The T-tops were disastrous. They all leaked,” he said about the popular 1970s option.


In a 1977-1979 Trans Am, the stick-shift came only with the T/A 6.6 engine, Pontiac’s code W72 400 cu.-in. performance option over the standard L78 400. An automatic, which was standard with the milder engine, was optional for the W72. Eddie’s TA had the Trans Am Special Performance Package that bundled the W72 motor with a comprehensive new-for-1978 WS6 chassis upgrade. A W72/WS6 Trans Am was as hot as a ponycar got in 1978. Eddie’s father, however, was not enthused by the acquisition.


“You traded for this?! Are you out of your mind?!” Eddie recalled him shouting.


Eli spotted the car’s problem right away. With either engine, a black Trans Am typically ordered for the dealer inventory would have the automatic, A/C, T-tops, stereo upgrade, and Trans Am Hood Decal, aka the “screaming chicken.”


“We ordered and sold a lot like that,” Eddie said. “You couldn’t ask for a better promo than that movie.”


Eddie’s Trans Am trade had only A/C, rear defroster, and roof drip moldings, but what really steamed his dad was the four-speed. With it, Eddie explained, the Trans Am was “basically sales-proof” in their corner of traffic-congested Metropolitan New York. Eddie didn’t care, because he’d intended to make the car his personal demo. It would have been a bargain at $6945 retail, about $1500-$2500 less than typically optioned-up Trans Ams and delivering L82 Corvette performance for $3500 less!


The W72 400 in Eddie’s TA has some 1960s Ram-Air III parts for even more power.


Courtesy Eddie Bloom


The W72 was Pontiac’s final 400, and it went out in fighting form. With help from dealership mechanics Ed Alessi and Butch Di Lorenzo (also a drag racer), Eddie fortified his Trans Am with the kind of “day two” mods that had made Myrtle Motors a magnet for New York-area Poncho fans and racers in the 1960s and early 1970s. (Myrtle Motors and its mechanics may be familiar to those who read about[Frank Kotnik’s ’76 Firebird Formula](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/formula-for-healing-frank-kotnicks-1976-pontiac-firebird-formula/) on Hagerty this past summer.)


They swapped in Pontiac’s #068 Ram Air III cam with 1.65:1 rockers, tweaked the Quadrajet carb’s jetting, and ditched the catalytic converter. For a bit more flash, Eddie had the dealership’s paint touch-up guy run a wide gold stripe down the car’s center.


“I’ve been driving the Trans Am ever since,” he said. “I ran it at Englishtown a couple of times. Today it’s a fun cruiser with about 29,000 miles and a few scrapes and bruises from when I drove it in Manhattan.”


Eddie had Myrtle Motors’ touch-up paint guy put the gold stripe on the birdless Trans Am.


Courtesy Eddie Bloom


## Growing Up with Pontiac Drag Racing


Founded by Eddie’s grandfather in 1935, Myrtle Motors began catering to the area’s racers in the ’60s with[Super Duty Catalinas](https://www.hagerty.com/media/archived/pontiac-super-duty/) and then the[GTO](https://www.hagerty.com/media/buying-and-selling/your-definitive-pontiac-gto-buyers-guide/) and[Firebird](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/your-handy-1970-81-pontiac-firebird-buyers-guide/) . Eddie, his dad, uncle, and cousins would watch drag races run with a flagman at Roosevelt’s Field airstrip in nearby Garden City. They’d root for Harry Wesch, Sr., a wiz mechanic and driver who campaigned a 1962 Super Duty Catalina he’d bought from Myrtle. Wesch later joined the dealer and managed its Hy-Performance Club, a customer program for speed parts, “Tiger” super-tunes, and powertrain mods. Myrtle’s special-build 428 H.O. Tiger engine swap gave 12-second quarter-mile performance in a Firebird or GTO, garnering East and West Coast magazine coverage.


The Myrtle Motors Hy-Performance Club was the ticket to be “leader of your pack” in the late ’60s.


Courtesy Eddie Bloom


The dealer contracted with local speed shops to install cams, valvetrains, shift kits for automatics, and other upgrades. Myrtle Motors even fielded its own NHRA C/Stock Automatic drag-race car, one of a short run of special ’67 Firebirds Eddie remembers Pontiac making for that purpose.


“They had the first-gen Ram-Air motors, bench seat, and no other options,” he said.


Wesch raced the Firebird extensively at National Speedway in Center Moriches and at tracks up and down the East Coast, becoming the car to beat in its class. Myrtle Motors and its Firebird caught the attention of New York-based Hi-Performance Cars magazine, known for its “tell-it-like-it-is” muscle car tests.


Myrtle Motors’ Firebird racer with Wesch’s “Tiger” 428 engine-swap Firebird.


Marty Schorr


Marty Schorr, who would later become Buick’s long-time East Coast PR rep, was the magazine’s editor-in-chief. Featuring Myrtle’s work, he explained, helped balance magazine coverage of Pontiacs tweaked by[Royal Pontiac](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/royal-pontiac/) in Michigan.


“I was glad to have a local Pontiac dealer doing that. I tried to give coverage to New York area shops and dealerships,” Schorr said. The magazine covered drag-strip action, and Schorr was also aware of the influence that illicit street racing had on the local muscle car market. Brooklyn and Queens had plenty of hot spots.


“What started out as guys running at Connecting Highway turned into some running for big money,” he said. “If you were someone like Harry Wesch, you wanted to be represented at these places, because it brought business into the dealership.”


Wesch would covertly join the street action with the “Myrtle Tiger” Firebird racer, taping paper over the dealer’s name on the car. When the disguise fell off, the police showed up.


Myrtle Motors campaigned a 1967 Firebird in NHRA C/Stock Automatic, with Harry Wesch driving, seen here at National Speedway on Long Island, NY.


Marty Schorr


“Dad had a sit-down visit at the dealership from NYPD highway department detectives,” Eddie said. “They threatened arrest. He really blew his cork, and the racecar was sold.”


Eddie enjoyed his own drag racing action at National with a ’64 GTO hot-rodded at Myrtle. He sold it when he left for the University of New Mexico in Albuquerque in 1972, driving a new GTO. At school, he majored in having fun.


“My dorm was on Central Avenue, which was the old Route 66, and it was like American Graffiti,” he said. “It was a wild and wonderful time.”


Eddie kept up that life until 1977. “Dad came out to New Mexico, grabbed me by the collar and dragged me back to New York. I didn’t go quietly,” he said. Eddie’s girlfriend, Cathryn, followed a while later. The two are celebrating their 45th wedding anniversary in October.


Eddie Bloom with his W72 Trans Am in 1986 and 2026.


Marty Schorr/Courtesy Eddie Bloom


## Factory Basics: 1977-1979 W72 Firebird Trans Am


Before *Smokey and the Bandit* brought added fame, Trans Am sales had been soaring since Pontiac slapped the giant bird on the hood[in 1973](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/trans-am-screaming-chicken-history/) . Emissions regulations had weakened performance considerably by 1976, when the Trans Am sold 49,000 units(!), but the car’s “gotta have it” appeal only grew stronger.


Pontiac kept up the good fight for horsepower, though. As the 200-hp L75 455 cubic-inch V-8 option departed after the 1976 model, a replacement waited in the wings. A June 1976 dealer bulletin announced a new LS7 400-cube performance engine package for the 1977 Formula and Trans Am, and it ultimately showed up as W72 on the order sheet.


June 1976 dealer bulletin alerted Pontiac dealers to the upcoming “LS7” engine option, which became “W72” on order sheets.


Courtesy John Witzke/POCI


Available with either the four-speed manual or TH350 three-speed automatic transmission, the first-year W72 matched the canceled 455’s horsepower and had nearly the same peak torque. At $12 less than the “screaming chicken” on the hood, the $50 W72 was a screaming deal *under* it. (The option cost $205 in the Firebird Formula, since it was a bigger step above that less expensive model’s standard 5.0-liter V-8.)


The Myrtle Motors dealer badge was once a hint that something extra might be under the hood.


Courtesy Eddie Bloom


The W72’s extra ponies came from good old-fashioned hotrodding. Cylinder head castings from Pontiac’s 350, which had the same valve sizes as the 400 but smaller combustion chambers, boosted compression a half-point to 8.1. The W72-specific cam had longer duration than the L78’s cam, and Pontiac tweaked the 800-cfm Quadrajet four-barrel carburetor and the HEI distributor’s advance curves to spread the power over a broader range.


Special chromoly piston rings, a 60-psi oil pump (vs. the L78’s 40), and a baffled oil pan catered to harder driving. Chrome valve covers were a classic muscle car touch. W72-equipped Trans Ams wore “T/A 6.6” decals on the non-functional shaker hood scoop, while the L78 or L80 Oldsmobile 403 both displayed “6.6 Litre.”


With either transmission, the Safe-T-Track limited-slip differential had a 3.23:1 axle ratio. Pontiac tweaked the automatic with higher converter stall speed and full-throttle shift points, 4800-4900 rpm vs. 4200 for the L78.


The W72 and WS6 options were eventually separated for 1978 Trans Ams, and the W72 ultimately became four-speed stick only.


Courtesy John Witzke/POCI


The W72 was a hit, with 26,177 out of 68,744 Trans Ams getting it for 1977, plus nearly 2500 Formulas. The Trans Am became the most popular Firebird that year, selling more than the base and Esprit models combined.


Camshaft revisions and a new semi-dual exhaust system boosted the 1978 W72’s output to 220 hp, with 320 lb.-ft. of peak torque at 2800 rpm. Replacing the single pipe from the catalytic converter back to a single transverse muffler, a new Y-pipe from the converter split into dual 2.25-inch pipes and dual resonators. Four-speed cars got a lower 3.42 axle ratio for added zip.


This 1978 W72/WS6 Trans Am has been Eddie Bloom’s pride since new.


Courtesy Eddie Bloom


Initially, the 1978 W72 engine was combined in the Trans Am Special Performance Package with a major chassis upgrade identified as WS6 on the build sheet. This package gave the Trans Am Corvette-baiting handling with quickened steering, a thicker rear anti-roll bar, stiffer rear springs, different shock tuning and bushings, and 15×8-inch cast-aluminum “snowflake” wheels with 225/70R15 radial tires. The cost was $324 on a base Trans Am but just $151 on the Special Editions, which already included the 8-inch wheels.


A February 22, 1978 Pontiac dealer bulletin announced separating the two options, the W72 for $75 and the WS6 chassis/wheel upgrade at $249. If the customer ordered both, the window sticker still showed the combined Trans Am Performance Package for $324, according to John Witzke, W72 Firebird Technical Advisor and Historian for the Pontiac Oakland Club International. (Witzke shared his research for this story.)


Eddie’s Trans Am was a performance bargain in 1978, with the T/A 6.6 motor for fun and A/C for New York summer comfort.


Courtesy Eddie Bloom


That same bulletin also announced the pending end of the automatic transmission option for the W72. A stick-shift was not sales-proof everywhere. Trans Am sales made another huge leap, this time by more than 35 percent to 93,341. Witzke’s research confirmed that 33,192 Trans Ams had the W72 engine, 12,692 of those getting the four-speed. There were 1694 W72 Formulas that year, and leftover W72 motors went into 8326 Trans Ams and 367 Formulas for 1979. All were four-speeds with a 3.23 axle ratio and now-mandatory WS6 chassis package for $534 total. Call that a profit-grab before the Pontiac 400, a star athlete in the muscle car era, headed into history.


Media road tests of 1978-1979 four-speed Trans Ams showed low 15-second quarter-mile times at 93-96 mph. Though not as quick as some pre-1975 versions, a W72 TA could dust a base Corvette and a Camaro Z28.


## Changing Times for Pontiac


Eddie races a ’68 Firebird in Super Street and has been campaigning an ’85 Trans Am (right) for nearly 40 years, currently with another driver.


Courtesy Eddie Bloom


In the 1980s, Myrtle maintained Pontiac’s New York-area media test car fleet. Eddie was racing a ’68 Firebird at National Speedway, and then he lucked into a special ’85 Trans Am that Pontiac had loaned to *Popular Mechanics* to modify for magazine features. The car came through Myrtle on its way back to GM to be crushed. Eddie bought it as scrap, with no title. He set up the car for NHRA Super Stock B/S and drove it through 2012. He still campaigns it with a different driver and still pilots his ’68 in Super Street.


Before Eddie and Cathryn had kids, they took the Trans Am on some long trips, including Charlottesville, Virginia, and North Carolina’s Outer Banks. The car mostly stayed in the garage after that. Eddie closed Myrtle Motors in 1992 during a tough time for auto retailing. He redeveloped the property into a successful shopping center and ultimately left the car business.


Hidden driving lights are useful on Upstate New York’s backroads.


Courtesy Eddie Bloom


These days, the ’78 Trans Am stays at Eddie’s getaway home in Upstate New York. For him, every drive rekindles memories of fast Pontiacs, drag racing, and the great racers and mechanics he called friends.


The Trans Am now makes memories for a new generation as Eddie takes his teenage grandson out for drives along the area’s twisty backroads. He got a laugh when the boy pointed to the stereo he’d installed decades ago, asking, “What’s that?”


When Eddie answered, “A cassette player,” his grandson fired back, “What’s a cassette player?”


Eddie popped in a tape he had in the glove compartment, and the still-functional tape deck cranked out the tunes as they blasted along with the volume up and the windows down.


“They say you can never have too much fun, but we must always try,” he said.


***


**Car:** **** 1978 Pontiac Firebird Trans Am W72/WS6


**Name:** **** Eddie Bloom


**Home:** Queens, New York


**Delivery date:** **** Spring, 1978


**Miles on car:** 29,000
